title: Confocal imaging from biphoton correlations
authors: Euan Millar, Emma Pearce, Daniele Faccio, Miles J. Padgett
abstract: Confocal microscopy provides optical sectioning for three-dimensional imaging but conventionally relies on point-by-point scanning and physical pinholes, limiting imaging speed. Here, we demonstrate that confocal sectioning can instead arise directly from quantum measurement, using spatial correlations in entangled biphoton states. Spatially resolved coincidence measurements in a widefield imaging system suppress contributions from out-of-focus planes, producing optical sectioning in parallel across the whole field of view without physical pinholes or mechanical scanning. In addition, this quantum approach obtains an axial response that, as a result of position-momentum entanglement, is $\sqrt{2}$-times narrower than that of classical confocal imaging. Our work establishes biphoton correlations as a mechanism for improved confocal imaging and enables parallel, pinhole-free optical sectioning without mechanical scanning.
summary: This paper demonstrates that optical sectioning, traditionally requiring physical pinholes or scanning, can be achieved purely through quantum measurement using entangled biphoton pairs. By measuring spatial correlations, the system naturally suppresses out-of-focus light, yielding an axial resolution significantly better than both classical and conventional quantum confocal methods. This establishes biphoton correlations as a powerful, pinhole-free mechanism for advanced microscopy.
main_problem: To demonstrate that the optical sectioning capability of confocal microscopy can arise directly from quantum measurement using spatial correlations in entangled biphoton states, eliminating the need for physical pinholes or mechanical scanning.
main_result: The quantum approach yields an axial point spread function (PSF) that is $\sqrt{2}$-times narrower than classical confocal imaging, achieving enhanced optical sectioning through the coherent combination of biphoton propagation phases.
method: The study combines theoretical analysis (using the advanced wave picture and coincidence probability derivations) with experimental measurements on biphoton imaging systems.
model_or_system: The system utilizes entangled biphoton states, typically generated via Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) in a BBO crystal, and measures coincidence counts in a widefield imaging setup.
key_observables: Coincidence count probability $G^{(2)}$, Axial Point Spread Function (PSF) width, and the second-order correlation function $g^{(2)}$ as a function of axial position ($z$).
important_parameters: The axial confinement is shown to be dependent on the transverse correlation bandwidth, and the enhancement factor is compared against classical ($\sqrt{2}$) and widefield (1) limits.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Klyshko interpretation, and comparisons are made assuming Gaussian beam profiles.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometric analogy between classical and quantum imaging, show simulated biphoton joint probability distributions, and present experimental measurements comparing coincidence signal degradation versus singles signal degradation under defocus and scattering.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the scientific problem by comparing classical and quantum methods, develops the theory using biphoton correlations, presents experimental setups and measurements comparing axial confinement, and concludes by quantifying the quantum advantage.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally verifiable demonstration of how fundamental quantum correlations (entanglement) can enhance classical imaging modalities, offering a quantum-enhanced tool for microscopy.

FIG. 3. Far-field biphoton imaging setup. A 355 nm pump laser is spatially filtered and directed onto a BBO crystal to generate spatially entangled photon pairs via type-II SPDC. The far-field of the down-converted biphoton is relayed (f1) through a demagnifying telescope (f2 and f3) and imaged onto an EMCCD camera, where two regions of interest, O1 and O2, are selected. A π rotation is applied to O2 to convert momentum anti-correlations into spatial correlations at the detector. Band-pass and long-pass filters select near-degenerate photon pairs, and the camera is scanned along the optical axis to record images at different focal planes.
